topics.kicker: Monotheistic religion from Punjab, India · Founded by Guru Nanak
topics.briefing: Every day, volunteers at the Golden Temple in Amritsar, India, cook free meals for huge crowds, who sit side by side on the floor no matter their religion or caste. That kitchen, called a langar, shows a core idea of Sikhism: everyone is equal before one God. The faith was founded by Guru Nanak around 1500, and today Sikhs honor their holy book, the Guru Granth Sahib, as their eternal Guru.

media.title: Sikhism
media.note: Quick read: Guru Nanak, the ten Gurus, beliefs, the Khalsa, and festivals

qb.tip: All 7 hits are on target, and nearly every one uses Punjab, Guru Nanak, the Adi Granth, or the Five Ks; skip one 2014 line that credits this faith with strict ahimsa, which is really a Jain hallmark.

sample.note: the 7 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: On the festival of Vaisakhi [“vy-SAH-kee”] in 1699, this religion’s tenth Guru asked who was willing to give his life for the faith, and five volunteers stepped forward. Those five, honored as the Panj Pyare [“punj pee-AH-ray”] or “Five Beloved Ones,” became the first members of the Khalsa, the order of initiated believers.
tossups.r: Many of its men wear turbans over uncut hair. For 10 points, name this religion founded by Guru Nanak in Punjab.

tossups.p: To name a baby in this religion, a family opens its holy book to a random page, and the child’s name begins with the first letter of the hymn read from that page. Girls are also given the name Kaur [“KOWR”], meaning “princess,” and boys are given Singh, meaning “lion.”
tossups.r: The holy book is the Guru Granth Sahib. For 10 points, name this faith founded by Guru Nanak.

tossups.p: This religion’s holy book opens with the Mul Mantar [“MOOL MUN-ter”], a short creed that begins with the words “Ik Onkar” [“ik OHN-kar”], meaning “One Creator.” Its fifth Guru, Arjan, compiled that book in 1604 and installed it in a temple he had built in Amritsar.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this monotheistic religion from Punjab, India, whose followers keep the Five Ks.

tossups.p: The founder of this religion vanished for three days while bathing in the Kali Bein [“KAH-lee BAYN”] river, then returned and announced, “There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim.” He then spent years traveling with Bhai Mardana [“BHY mar-DAH-nuh”], a Muslim musician who played a stringed instrument called the rabab.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this religion begun by Guru Nanak, whose holiest site is the Golden Temple.

tossups.p: This religion’s emblem, the khanda [“KHUN-dah”], shows a double-edged sword set over a ring-shaped weapon called a chakkar, between two curved swords. That emblem decorates the Nishan Sahib [“nee-SHAHN SAH-hib”], a triangular saffron flag that flies on a tall pole outside its houses of worship, called gurdwaras.
tossups.r: It was founded by Guru Nanak. For 10 points, name this religion whose men often take the last name Singh.

tossups.p: In this religion, a reader called a granthi [“GRUN-tee”] looks after the holy book, but any member of the congregation may lead the prayers. During readings, an attendant waves a whisk called a chaur [“CHOWR”] over that book as a sign of respect, and the book is wrapped in decorated cloths when it is closed.
tossups.r: The tenth Guru declared that book, the Guru Granth Sahib, the final Guru. For 10 points, name this religion of Punjab.

tossups.p: This religion’s second leader, Guru Angad [“UNG-gud”], is credited with standardizing the Gurmukhi [“GOOR-moo-kee”] script, which is used to write Punjabi in India. Angad’s wife, Mata Khivi [“KEE-vee”], is honored for running a free kitchen where visitors of any background sit and eat together.
tossups.r: Those kitchens, called langars, are found at its houses of worship. For 10 points, name this religion whose first Guru was Nanak.

tossups.p: This religion’s sixth Guru, Hargobind, wore two swords, miri [“MEE-ree”] and piri [“PEE-ree”], to show that he held both worldly and spiritual authority. Facing this religion’s holiest shrine, Hargobind built the Akal Takht [“uh-KAAL TUKHT”], or “Throne of the Timeless One,” which is still a seat of authority for its community.
tossups.r: That shrine is the Golden Temple in Amritsar. For 10 points, name this religion whose holy book is the Guru Granth Sahib.

tossups.p: In the Amrit Sanchar [“UM-rit sun-CHAR”] ceremony, believers joining this religion’s Khalsa drink sweetened water stirred with a double-edged sword. They promise to follow its code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada [“REH-hut mur-YAH-dah”], and to recite morning prayers called the Five Banis [“BAH-neez”].
tossups.r: They must also wear a steel bracelet called a kara and keep a wooden comb called a kanga. For 10 points, name this religion founded by Guru Nanak.

tossups.p: Hymns by the poet-saint Kabir and the Sufi mystic Sheikh Farid appear in this religion’s scripture, which is arranged mostly by musical modes called ragas. A nonstop reading of all 1,430 pages of that scripture, called an Akhand Path [“UH-khund PAHT”], takes about 48 hours.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this religion whose scripture, the Adi Granth, is honored as its eternal Guru.

tossups.p: Maharaja Ranjit Singh, the “Lion of Punjab,” had the upper floors of this religion’s holiest shrine covered in gold. That shrine, the Harmandir Sahib [“HUR-mun-deer SAH-hib”], stands in the middle of a sacred pool and has four entrances, a sign that people from every direction are welcome.
tossups.r: Its kitchen serves free meals to huge crowds every day. For 10 points, name this religion whose holiest site is the Golden Temple in Amritsar.

tossups.p: In 2019, a visa-free corridor opened so that pilgrims from India could cross into Pakistan to visit Kartarpur, where this religion’s founder spent his final years. That founder taught three main duties: remember God’s name, earn an honest living, and share with people in need.
tossups.r: Its followers call God Waheguru [“wah-hay-GOO-roo”]. For 10 points, name this religion founded by Guru Nanak in Punjab.

tossups.p: Before his death in 1708, this religion’s tenth Guru announced that there would be no more human Gurus and that its scripture would guide believers forever. That leader, Gobind Singh, had earlier founded the order of initiated believers called the Khalsa.
tossups.r: Khalsa members keep five articles of faith, including uncut hair and a small sword called a kirpan. For 10 points, name this religion whose holy city is Amritsar.

tossups.p: This religion’s third Guru, Amar Das, asked every visitor to eat in his free kitchen before meeting him, and the Mughal emperor Akbar is said to have sat on the floor and eaten there with everyone else. Volunteers still cook free meals at its houses of worship.
tossups.r: Those kitchens are called langars. For 10 points, name this religion whose male followers often take the name Singh, meaning “lion.”

tossups.p: This religion’s fourth Guru, Ram Das, founded a city and began digging a sacred pool there, and his youngest son and successor, Arjan, built a shrine in the middle of that pool. Arjan is honored as this religion’s first martyr; he died in 1606 while imprisoned by the Mughal emperor Jahangir.
tossups.r: That city is Amritsar. For 10 points, name this religion whose holiest site there is the Golden Temple.

clues.t: A monotheistic religion from the Punjab region; most followers live in the Indian state of Punjab
Founded by Guru Nanak (1469–1539), the first of ten human Gurus
Holiest site: the Golden Temple, or Harmandir Sahib, in the city of Amritsar
Many followers, especially men, wear a turban over uncut hair (kesh)
Initiated believers keep the Five Ks, five articles of faith whose names all start with K
Holy book: the Guru Granth Sahib (Adi Granth), honored as the final, eternal Guru
The Khalsa: the order of initiated believers, founded in 1699
Guru Gobind Singh, the 10th Guru, founded the Khalsa and named the holy book the Guru before he died (1708)
The kirpan, a small curved sword or dagger, is one of the Five Ks
Other Ks: the kara (steel bracelet), kanga (wooden comb), and kachera (cotton shorts)
Men take the name Singh (“lion”); women take the name Kaur (“princess”)
Langar: a free community kitchen where everyone sits and eats together, whatever their caste or religion
Gurdwara (“door to the Guru”): its house of worship
Amrit Sanchar: the initiation ceremony, where believers drink amrit, sweetened water stirred with a double-edged sword
Panj Pyare (“Five Beloved Ones”): the five volunteers who became the first Khalsa members on Vaisakhi, 1699
“Ik Onkar” (“One Creator”) begins the Mul Mantar, the first words of the holy book
Guru Ram Das founded Amritsar; his son Guru Arjan, the 5th Guru, built the Harmandir Sahib and compiled the Adi Granth (1604)
Nanak said “There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim” after vanishing in the Kali Bein river; he traveled with Mardana, a Muslim rabab player
The khanda emblem: a double-edged sword over a ring (chakkar) between two curved swords; it flies on the Nishan Sahib flag
Naming ceremony: the holy book is opened at random, and the baby’s name starts with the first letter of the hymn
A granthi reads and cares for the holy book, but any member may lead prayers; a whisk (chaur) is waved over the book
Guru Hargobind, the 6th Guru, wore two swords, miri and piri (worldly and spiritual power), and built the Akal Takht
Guru Angad, the 2nd Guru, standardized the Gurmukhi script, used for the holy book and for Punjabi in India
Initiated believers recite the Five Banis, daily morning prayers that begin with Nanak’s Japji Sahib
The Rehat Maryada is its official code of conduct
Its scripture also holds hymns by Kabir and the Sufi Sheikh Farid; its 1,430 pages are arranged by ragas
Maharaja Ranjit Singh, the “Lion of Punjab,” covered the Golden Temple’s upper floors in gold; it has four entrances, open to all

trap.title: Which Indian religion?
trap.body: Sikhism, Hinduism, Jainism, and Buddhism all began in South Asia, and all four teach ideas like karma and rebirth, so early buzzes on “this Indian religion” often go wrong. Hearing “guru” is not enough either, because Hindu teachers are called gurus too. And a strict-nonviolence (ahimsa) clue points to Jainism, not Sikhism.
trap.fix: Wait for a clue only Sikhism has: Guru Nanak, the ten Gurus, the Guru Granth Sahib (Adi Granth), the Five Ks, the Khalsa, langar, the Golden Temple in Amritsar, or the names Singh and Kaur. Mahavira, the 24 Tirthankaras, and strict ahimsa mean Jainism.
trap.line: Real answer lines: Sikhism [or Sikhi] and Sikh (accept word forms like Sikhism or Sikhi)

topics.kicker: Ancient Indian religion of Mahavira · Famous for ahimsa (nonviolence)
topics.briefing: Some Jain monks gently sweep the ground in front of them with a soft broom, and some wear a cloth over their mouths, all to avoid harming even the tiniest insect. That care comes from ahimsa, or nonviolence, the central teaching of Jainism, an ancient religion of India. Jains honor 24 great teachers called Tirthankaras; the last, Mahavira, lived around the same time as the Buddha.

media.title: Jainism
media.note: Quick read: Mahavira, the 24 Tirthankaras, ahimsa, the sects, and festivals

qb.tip: Only 1 of the 2 Middle School/Easy High School hits is really about this religion (the other wants the color white), so we added 12 Regular High School tossups, and nearly all of them end with Mahavira, the 24 Tirthankaras, ahimsa, and the sky-clad and white-clad sects.

sample.note: 13 real QBReader tossups (1 Middle School/Easy High School + 12 Regular High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: One sect of this religion teaches that its 19th great teacher, Mallinath [“MUH-lee-naht”], was a woman, while another sect teaches that women must be reborn as men before they can reach liberation. That second sect’s monks give up nearly all possessions, even clothing, and are called “sky-clad,” or Digambara [“dig-UM-buh-ruh”].
tossups.r: Its last great teacher was Mahavira. For 10 points, name this Indian religion that teaches ahimsa, or nonviolence.

tossups.p: This religion’s idea of anekantavada [“uh-nay-kahn-tuh-VAH-duh”], or “many-sidedness,” teaches that the truth has many sides and no single view can capture all of it. Teachers often explain that idea with the story of several blind men who each touch a different part of an elephant and describe it differently.
tossups.r: Its two main sects are the Digambara and the Svetambara. For 10 points, name this religion whose 24th Tirthankara, Mahavira, taught nonviolence.

tossups.p: This religion’s official emblem shows a raised hand with a wheel on its palm, a reminder to stop and think before harming any living thing. Above the hand is an ancient Indian good-luck sign called a swastika.
tossups.r: Three dots above that sign stand for this religion’s Three Jewels. For 10 points, name this religion of Mahavira, whose followers practice ahimsa.

tossups.p: According to one tradition, a long famine forced the monk Bhadrabahu [“bud-ruh-BAH-hoo”] to lead his followers to southern India, and the emperor Chandragupta Maurya gave up his throne to go with them. One sect of this religion believes that its original scriptures, the Agamas, were lost during that period.
tossups.r: That sect is the “sky-clad” Digambara. For 10 points, name this religion whose 24th and last Tirthankara was Mahavira.

tossups.p: Born a prince named Vardhamana [“vur-duh-MAH-nuh”], this religion’s most recent great teacher left home at about 30 and spent more than twelve years fasting and meditating. He then reached kevala jnana [“KAY-vuh-luh JNAH-nuh”], a state of perfect, all-knowing wisdom, and spent the rest of his life teaching.
tossups.r: That teacher was Mahavira, the 24th Tirthankara. For 10 points, name this Indian religion that stresses ahimsa.

tossups.p: Every twelve years, worshippers in this religion pour milk, saffron, and other offerings over a giant statue of Bahubali [“BAH-hoo-bah-lee”], carved from a single block of granite, at Shravanabelagola [“shruh-vuh-nuh-BEL-uh-go-luh”]. That statue shows Bahubali standing so still in meditation that vines have wrapped around his legs.
tossups.r: Its followers honor 24 Tirthankaras, ending with Mahavira. For 10 points, name this religion known for ahimsa.

tossups.p: On the last day of the festival of Paryushana [“par-YOO-shuh-nuh”], followers of this religion ask forgiveness from everyone they may have hurt during the past year, often saying “Micchami Dukkadam.” That festival comes near the end of summer.
tossups.r: Many believers fast and practice a meditation called samayika [“SAH-mah-yee-kuh”] during that festival. For 10 points, name this religion whose two main sects are the Digambara and the Svetambara.

tossups.p: In this religion’s most important prayer, the Namokar Mantra [“nuh-MOH-kar MUN-truh”], believers bow to five kinds of supreme beings, including perfected souls, spiritual leaders, and monks. The prayer does not ask any god for favors, because this religion teaches that the universe was never created and has no creator god.
tossups.r: Instead, believers honor 24 Tirthankaras, or “ford-makers.” For 10 points, name this Indian religion of Mahavira, known for its strict nonviolence.

tossups.p: This religion pictures the universe as a giant figure of a person standing with legs apart and hands on hips, divided into three worlds. Souls that escape the cycle of rebirth rise to the very top of that universe, where they live forever in perfect knowledge and bliss.
tossups.r: Its 24 great teachers ended with Mahavira. For 10 points, name this religion that stresses ahimsa, or nonviolence.

tossups.p: Statues of this religion’s 23rd great teacher, Parshvanatha [“parsh-vuh-NAH-tuh”], whom many historians consider a real person, often show a many-headed cobra spreading its hood over his head. This religion’s first such teacher, Rishabhanatha [“rish-uh-buh-NAH-tuh”], is said to have taught humans farming, writing, and other skills.
tossups.r: Its 24th such teacher was Mahavira. For 10 points, name this religion whose great teachers are called Tirthankaras.

tossups.p: As a young man, Mohandas Gandhi was deeply influenced by Shrimad Rajchandra [“SHREE-mud raj-CHUN-druh”], a poet and thinker from this religion, and Gandhi later drew on its idea of nonviolence in India’s struggle for independence. Its monks and nuns take five great vows, including truthfulness and not stealing.
tossups.r: Another vow, aparigraha [“uh-puh-ree-GRUH-huh”], means owning nothing beyond what is needed. For 10 points, name this religion whose 24th Tirthankara was Mahavira.

tossups.p: Strict followers of this religion avoid eating onions, garlic, and potatoes, because digging up root vegetables harms the many tiny living things in the soil. Many also eat only before sunset, and some drink only boiled water, all to limit harm to even the smallest creatures.
tossups.r: They are strict vegetarians who practice ahimsa. For 10 points, name this religion of the 24 Tirthankaras.

tossups.p: Some monks of this religion wear a cloth called a muhapatti [“moo-huh-PUT-tee”] over their mouths so they will not breathe in or harm tiny insects. Monks also carry a soft broom to gently sweep the path in front of them, and the “sky-clad” monks use a whisk made of peacock feathers.
tossups.r: Those “sky-clad” monks belong to the Digambara sect. For 10 points, name this religion of ahimsa, whose last Tirthankara was Mahavira.

tossups.p: This religion takes its name from jina [“JIN-uh”], a word meaning “conqueror,” for teachers who conquered their own anger, greed, and desires. It teaches that karma is a sticky, invisible substance that clings to the soul, and that the soul becomes free only after all of that karma is shed.
tossups.r: Its path to freedom requires the Three Jewels: right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct. For 10 points, name this religion of Mahavira.

tossups.p: Followers of this religion celebrate Diwali as the anniversary of the night their 24th great teacher reached moksha, or final liberation, at Pawapuri [“PAH-vah-poo-ree”] in eastern India. They also celebrate that teacher’s birthday each spring, and many visit the hilltop temples of Palitana [“PAH-lee-tah-nuh”] on pilgrimage.
tossups.r: That teacher was Mahavira. For 10 points, name this Indian religion known for its vow of nonviolence, or ahimsa.

clues.t: Its central teaching is ahimsa: nonviolence toward every living thing, even the tiniest insects
Mahavira, its 24th and last Tirthankara, lived in India around 500 BCE, about the same time as the Buddha
Honors 24 Tirthankaras (“ford-makers”), teachers who found a way across the river of rebirth
An ancient religion from India; most of its followers still live there
Two main sects: Digambara (“sky-clad”) monks give up even clothing; Svetambara (“white-clad”) monks wear white robes
Some monks wear a mouth cloth (muhapatti) and sweep the path with a soft broom so they never harm insects
Strictly vegetarian; many also avoid root vegetables like onions and potatoes, since digging them up harms tiny living things
Karma is a sticky, invisible substance that clings to the soul (jiva); shedding all of it frees the soul
Paryushana: its most important festival, a late-summer time of fasting that ends with asking everyone’s forgiveness
Teaches that the universe was never created and has no creator god
Its name comes from jina (“conqueror”), a soul that has conquered anger, greed, and desire
Three Jewels (ratnatraya): right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct
Monks and nuns take five great vows, and laypeople keep milder versions; they include ahimsa, truthfulness, not stealing, and aparigraha (owning nothing beyond what is needed)
Celebrates Diwali as the night Mahavira reached moksha (final liberation) at Pawapuri
Anekantavada (“many-sidedness”): truth has many sides, like the blind men who each touch a different part of an elephant
Digambaras say women must be reborn as men to reach liberation; Svetambaras say the 19th Tirthankara, Mallinath, was a woman
Agamas: its scriptures; Digambaras believe the originals were lost during a famine
Kevala jnana: perfect, all-knowing wisdom; souls who reach it are called kevalins
Its emblem: a raised hand with a wheel on the palm (stop and think before harming), plus a swastika, an ancient Indian good-luck sign
Samayika: a period of calm meditation, often practiced during Paryushana
Rishabhanatha was the 1st Tirthankara; Parshvanatha, the 23rd, is shown under a many-headed cobra hood
Chandragupta Maurya, founder of the Maurya Empire, is said to have given up his throne to become one of its monks
The Namokar Mantra, its most important prayer, bows to five kinds of supreme beings
Its universe is shaped like a giant person standing with legs apart, divided into three worlds; freed souls rise to the top
The giant granite statue of Bahubali at Shravanabelagola is bathed in milk and saffron every 12 years
Its ahimsa influenced Mahatma Gandhi, whose mentor Shrimad Rajchandra followed this faith

trap.title: Mahavira or the Buddha?
trap.body: Jainism and Buddhism were born in the same part of India at about the same time, and both teach karma, rebirth, and nonviolence, so players often mix them up. Mahavira and the Buddha (Siddhartha Gautama) were even alive at the same time. An ahimsa clue alone is not enough either, because Hindus, Buddhists, and Gandhi also taught nonviolence.
trap.fix: Listen for words only Jainism uses: Tirthankara, Mahavira, Digambara (“sky-clad”) and Svetambara (“white-clad”), anekantavada, or monks with mouth cloths and brooms. Bodhisattvas, the Four Noble Truths, the Eightfold Path, and Theravada or Mahayana mean Buddhism.

topics.kicker: Ancient Persian faith of Zoroaster · One of the oldest living religions
topics.briefing: In some temples in India and Iran, sacred fires have been kept burning for centuries, tended day and night by priests. Those fires are symbols of goodness and light in Zoroastrianism, one of the world’s oldest religions, founded in ancient Persia by the prophet Zoroaster. Its followers believe the good god Ahura Mazda is locked in a struggle with the evil spirit Angra Mainyu, and each person must choose a side.

media.note: Quick read: Zoroaster, Ahura Mazda and Ahriman, prayers, festivals, and the Parsis

qb.tip: All 5 Middle School/Easy High School hits are on target, and the 12 Regular High School ones we added show the same core (Ahura Mazda, Angra Mainyu, the Avesta, fire temples, and Towers of Silence), but no answer line we found accepts “Parsi.”

sample.note: 17 real QBReader tossups (5 Middle School/Easy High School + 12 Regular High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: A symbol of this religion called the Faravahar [“fah-RAH-vah-har”] shows a bearded man rising from a disc with outspread wings, and it has become a symbol of Iran itself. Its followers pray facing a source of light, such as a sacred fire.
tossups.r: They try to live by the motto “good thoughts, good words, good deeds.” For 10 points, name this ancient Persian religion whose supreme god is Ahura Mazda.

tossups.p: Followers of this religion are urged to choose asha [“AH-shuh”], meaning truth and right order, over druj [“drooj”], meaning the lie. That struggle mirrors the cosmic battle between its good creator god and the destructive spirit Angra Mainyu [“AHN-gruh MINE-yoo”], also called Ahriman [“AH-ree-mahn”].
tossups.r: Nowruz, the Persian New Year, has roots in this faith. For 10 points, name this ancient Persian religion founded by the prophet Zarathustra.

tossups.p: In this religion, two four-eyed dogs guard the Chinvat [“CHIN-vaht”] Bridge, which every soul must cross after death. The bridge grows wide for the righteous, who reach the House of Song, but becomes as narrow as a blade for the wicked, who fall into the House of Lies.
tossups.r: Its holy book is the Avesta. For 10 points, name this religion whose followers worship Ahura Mazda in fire temples.

tossups.p: At the end of time in this religion, a savior called the Saoshyant [“SOWSH-yant”] will help bring about Frashokereti [“frah-sho-keh-REH-tee”], a final renewal of the world. The dead will rise, and everyone will pass through a river of molten metal that feels like warm milk to the righteous.
tossups.r: Some scholars think these ideas influenced Judaism and Christianity. For 10 points, name this Persian religion whose holy book is the Avesta.

tossups.p: According to tradition, this religion’s founder was about 30 years old and fetching water from a river when Vohu Manah [“VOH-hoo MAH-nah”], or “Good Mind,” appeared to him in a vision. Vohu Manah is one of six divine helpers of the supreme god called the Amesha Spentas [“AH-meh-shuh SPEN-tuhz”], or “Bounteous Immortals.”
tossups.r: That founder later composed hymns called the Gathas. For 10 points, name this ancient Persian religion founded by Zoroaster.

tossups.p: During the Navjote [“nuv-JOHT”] ceremony, children in this religion are given a white cotton undershirt called a sudreh [“SOOD-ray”] and a sacred cord called a kusti [“KUSH-tee”], which is woven from 72 threads and tied around the waist. Followers retie the kusti during daily prayers.
tossups.r: The ceremony marks a child’s entry into the faith. For 10 points, name this religion of the Parsis, known for its fire temples and Towers of Silence.

tossups.p: A heresy within this religion taught that a god of infinite time named Zurvan [“ZUR-vahn”] was the father of twin spirits, one good and one evil. Mainstream followers instead teach that the good creator has always existed and will defeat the destructive spirit Angra Mainyu at the end of time.
tossups.r: That good creator is Ahura Mazda. For 10 points, name this dualistic religion from ancient Persia, founded by Zarathustra.

tossups.p: In this religion, fire, or atar [“AH-tar”], is honored as a sacred symbol of the creator’s light and purity. Its holiest temple fires, called Atash Behram [“AH-tush BEH-rum”], are consecrated with fires from many sources, including one started by lightning.
tossups.r: One such fire in Udvada, India, is said to have burned for more than a thousand years. For 10 points, name this religion of Persia that honors Ahura Mazda.

tossups.p: A popular legend says that when refugees from this religion reached western India, a local ruler sent them a full bowl of milk to show there was no room, and their priest stirred in sugar to show they would sweeten the land without overflowing it.
tossups.r: Their descendants, the Parsis, still live mainly around Mumbai. For 10 points, name this religion that began in Persia.

tossups.p: Before he became the lead singer of the rock band Queen, Freddie Mercury grew up as Farrokh Bulsara in a family that followed this religion, and his funeral service was led by one of its priests. Other famous members of this faith include the Tata family, who built one of India’s biggest companies.
tossups.r: Its members in India are called Parsis. For 10 points, name this ancient religion founded by Zoroaster in Persia.

tossups.p: Richard Strauss wrote a famous tone poem, used at the start of the film _2001: A Space Odyssey_, based on a book by Friedrich Nietzsche named for this religion’s founder. In that book, a fictional version of the founder comes down from the mountains to preach about the “Übermensch.”
tossups.r: That book is _Thus Spoke Zarathustra_. For 10 points, name this Persian religion whose supreme god is Ahura Mazda.

tossups.p: In the Behistun [“bay-hiss-TOON”] Inscription, the Persian king Darius I declared that he ruled by the favor of this religion’s supreme god. Centuries later, this religion became the official faith of the Sasanian [“suh-SAH-nee-un”] Empire, whose coins showed fire altars.
tossups.r: Arab armies conquered Persia in the 600s, and Islam gradually replaced it. For 10 points, name this ancient Persian religion whose god is Ahura Mazda.

tossups.p: Priests of this religion were called magi [“MAY-jy”], and the “wise men” who visit the baby Jesus in the Gospel of Matthew are often thought to have been such priests. Its scripture includes the Vendidad [“ven-dee-DAHD”], a book of purity laws and rules for driving away demons.
tossups.r: Its holy book is the Avesta. For 10 points, name this Persian religion that worships in fire temples.

tossups.p: Traditionally, followers of this religion placed their dead on stone towers called dakhmas [“DOCK-muhz”], open to the sun and to vultures, so that burial or cremation would not pollute the sacred earth or fire. In recent decades, a sharp drop in India’s vulture population has pushed the Parsis of Mumbai to look for other methods.
tossups.r: Those towers are known as Towers of Silence. For 10 points, name this Persian religion whose god is Ahura Mazda.

tossups.p: The oldest part of this religion’s scripture is a set of 17 hymns called the Gathas [“GAH-tuhz”], which are believed to have been composed by its founder himself. Those hymns are recited during the Yasna [“YUSS-nuh”], this religion’s main act of worship, and are written in an ancient language called Avestan.
tossups.r: Its scripture is the Avesta. For 10 points, name this religion founded by the Persian prophet Zarathustra.

clues.t: An ancient religion from Persia (modern Iran)
Its supreme god is Ahura Mazda, the “Wise Lord”
Founded by the prophet Zoroaster, also called Zarathustra
Dualistic: the good Ahura Mazda battles the evil spirit Angra Mainyu, also called Ahriman
Holy book: the Avesta (commentaries on it are called the Zend)
Worships in fire temples; fire is honored as a sacred symbol of the god’s light and purity
Traditionally, the dead were laid on stone Towers of Silence (dakhmas), open to the sky and to vultures, to keep earth and fire pure
After death, souls cross the Chinvat Bridge, guarded by two four-eyed dogs; it is wide for the good and narrow for the wicked
The good go to the House of Song; the wicked go to the House of Lies
Parsis: followers who fled Persia for India over a thousand years ago (legend: like sugar in milk); most now live around Mumbai
Motto: “good thoughts, good words, good deeds”
Nietzsche’s _Thus Spoke Zarathustra_ is named for its founder; Richard Strauss based a famous tone poem on that book
Its priests were called magi; the Bible’s “wise men” may have been magi
Its ideas of heaven and hell, a final judgment, and a coming savior may have influenced Judaism and Christianity
The Gathas: 17 hymns believed to be by the founder himself, recited in the Yasna, the main act of worship
Asha (truth and right order) is opposed by druj (the lie)
The Faravahar, a bearded man rising from a winged disc, is its best-known symbol
A future savior, the Saoshyant, will bring Frashokereti, the final renewal of the world, when the dead rise
Six Amesha Spentas (“Bounteous Immortals”) serve the supreme god; one, Vohu Manah (“Good Mind”), appeared to the founder in a vision
Zurvanism, a heresy, made Zurvan (infinite time) the father of twin good and evil spirits
Navjote: a child’s initiation, receiving the sudreh (white undershirt) and kusti (a cord of 72 threads)
Atar is sacred fire; the holiest temple fires, Atash Behram, are made from many fires, including one from lightning
The Vendidad, part of the Avesta, holds purity laws and rules against demons (daevas)
Achaemenid kings such as Darius I honored Ahura Mazda; later it was the official religion of the Sasanian Empire
Famous Parsis: Queen singer Freddie Mercury and the Tata family of business leaders
Nowruz, the Persian New Year celebrated at the spring equinox, has roots in this faith

trap.title: Not Manichaeism or Mithraism
trap.body: Several ancient religions from Persia and the Roman world get mixed up in tossups. Manichaeism, founded by the prophet Mani in the 200s CE, also taught a battle between light and darkness, and Mithraism was a Roman mystery religion built around the god Mithras. Some players also answer “Parsi,” but Parsis are the followers who settled in India, and no real answer line we found accepts it.
trap.fix: Ahura Mazda, Angra Mainyu, the Avesta and Gathas, fire temples, Towers of Silence, the Chinvat Bridge, and the Faravahar all mean Zoroastrianism. Mani, the “Religion of Light,” and Saint Augustine’s early years mean Manichaeism; Mithras and underground Roman temples called mithraea mean Mithraism.
trap.line: Real answer line: Zoroastrianism [or Mazdayasna or Mazdaism before “Mazda” is read; accept Zarathustrianism before “Zarathustra” is read]

topics.kicker: Haitian faith · Blends West African lwa worship with Catholic saints
topics.briefing: Beneath a top hat and tails, the spirit Baron Samedi watches over the dead in a real religion practiced by millions across Haiti and its diaspora. Vodou grew when enslaved West Africans blended their traditions with Catholicism, worshipping a distant creator, Bondye, through hundreds of approachable spirits called lwa. Priests called houngans and priestesses called mambos lead drumming ceremonies where dancers may become possessed — a far cry from Hollywood’s dolls and curses.

tossups.p: One spirit in this religion wears three wedding bands, symbolizing her marriages to three other spirits, including the warrior Ogou and the serpent spirit Damballa [“dahm-bah-LAH”]. That spirit of love and beauty, Erzulie [“air-ZOO-lee”], is one of hundreds of spirits called lwa that believers honor.
tossups.r: Those spirits connect worshippers to a distant creator called Bondye. For 10 points, name this Haitian religion, which does not actually focus on cursing dolls.

tossups.p: A 1791 ceremony at Bois Caïman [“bwah ky-MAHN”], led by figures of this religion, is widely remembered as a spark for the uprising that won Haiti’s independence. Priests called houngans and priestesses called mambos have long led this religion’s ceremonies of drumming, song, and dance.
tossups.r: Its supreme god, Bondye, is reached only through spirits called lwa. For 10 points, name this religion, whose practitioners do not really use pins and dolls to curse people.

tossups.p: Tradition in this religion holds that every person’s soul has two linked parts, called the gros bon ange and the ti bon ange. Initiated priests and priestesses carry a sacred beaded rattle, the asson, and may undergo possession by a spirit during ceremonies.
tossups.r: Those spirits, called lwa, include Baron Samedi and Papa Legba. For 10 points, name this Haitian religion that blends West African traditions with Catholicism.

tossups.p: A specialist called a bokor is sometimes hired in this religion for darker magic, unlike the community-serving priests and priestesses. Protective charm bags called gris-gris [“GREE-gree”] are part of a related tradition that took root in Louisiana, where Marie Laveau became a famous 19th-century priestess.
tossups.r: This religion’s main form developed in Haiti, blending Catholic and West African beliefs. For 10 points, name this religion, which doesn’t really revolve around cursing dolls.

tossups.p: Before many ceremonies in this religion, believers draw geometric patterns called veves [“vay-VAYS”] on the ground to invite a particular spirit to attend. One such spirit, Papa Legba, guardian of crossroads and gates, is traditionally saluted first.
tossups.r: Drumming and dance can lead worshippers to be possessed by one of these spirits, called lwa. For 10 points, name this Haitian religion.

tossups.p: Becoming a priest or priestess in this religion requires an initiation called the kanzo, which includes ritual seclusion and a symbolic washing of the head. Initiates then carry a sacred rattle called an asson.
tossups.r: Those priests, called houngans and mambos, lead ceremonies honoring spirits known as lwa. For 10 points, name this religion practiced mainly in Haiti.

tossups.p: The Ghede family of spirits in this religion, linked to death and ancestors, is often represented by a cross standing over a tomb. The head of that family, Baron Samedi, is usually pictured in a top hat, tails, and dark glasses.
tossups.r: He and other lwa connect believers to a distant creator called Bondye. For 10 points, name this Haitian religion, which is often unfairly reduced to zombies and dolls in movies.

tossups.p: Spirits in this religion are organized into groups called “nations,” including the gentle Rada and the fierier Petwo [“PET-wo”]. Most of these spirits are also linked to Catholic saints, a result of enslaved West Africans blending their beliefs with Catholicism under colonial rule.
tossups.r: Priests called houngans and priestesses called mambos lead this religion’s ceremonies. For 10 points, name this religion whose spirits are called lwa.

tossups.p: A jar called a govi is used in this religion to hold and honor the spirit of someone who has died. Spirits in this religion, called lwa, serve as go-betweens for a distant creator god whose French-derived name, Bondye, means “good god.”
tossups.r: They include Papa Legba and the top-hatted Baron Samedi. For 10 points, name this religion of Haiti, which doesn’t actually use pins and dolls to curse people.

tossups.p: A serpent spirit linked to water, Damballa, is honored in this religion alongside hundreds of other lwa. This religion’s priests, called houngans, and priestesses, called mambos, lead ceremonies of drumming, song, and dance that can end in spirit possession.
tossups.r: A related tradition took root in Louisiana, home to the famous priestess Marie Laveau. For 10 points, name this Haitian religion.

tossups.p: A warrior spirit tied to iron and weapons, Ogou [“oh-GOO”], is especially honored by soldiers and metalworkers in this religion. Spirits here are called lwa, and they connect believers to a distant creator known as Bondye.
tossups.r: This religion developed in Haiti by blending West African traditions with Catholicism. For 10 points, name this religion, which doesn’t really revolve around cursing dolls.

tossups.p: Marie Laveau became a famous 19th-century priestess of a Louisiana branch of this religion in New Orleans. Its main form developed in Haiti, where priests called houngans and priestesses called mambos lead worshippers in drumming, song, and dance.
tossups.r: Believers honor spirits called lwa, including Baron Samedi and Papa Legba. For 10 points, name this religion, which doesn’t actually focus on cursing dolls.

tossups.p: Baron Samedi, lord of the dead and cemeteries in this religion, is traditionally pictured in a top hat, tails, and dark glasses, smoking a cigar. He is one of hundreds of spirits called lwa who connect believers to the distant creator Bondye.
tossups.r: Priests called houngans and priestesses called mambos lead this religion’s drumming ceremonies. For 10 points, name this religion of Haiti, often unfairly linked to zombies and dolls in movies.

tossups.p: Papa Legba, the guardian of crossroads and gates, is traditionally saluted first at ceremonies in this religion, which honors hundreds of spirits called lwa. Those spirits serve as go-betweens for a distant, rarely-approached creator called Bondye.
tossups.r: This religion blends West African traditions with Roman Catholicism. For 10 points, name this religion practiced in Haiti and in Louisiana, which does not actually use pins and dolls to curse people.

tossups.p: Priests called houngans and priestesses called mambos lead this religion’s ceremonies of drumming, singing, and dance, which can end in spirit possession. Believers honor hundreds of spirits called lwa, who connect them to a distant creator, Bondye.

trap.title: Dolls are another answer line
trap.body: Because the real-world stereotype about pins and dolls is so well known, some tossups are actually about “dolls” as an object (accepting kachina dolls or voodoo dolls), not about this religion — don’t blurt the religion’s name when the question wants the object. It’s also easy to confuse this religion with Santería (Cuban, orishas and santeros) or Hoodoo (an American folk-magic practice with no temples or formal priesthood), which share African roots but are not the same tradition.
trap.fix: If the question asks “name this religion” and mentions Bondye, lwa, houngans, or mambos, answer “Voodoo” or “Vodou.” If it asks “name this object” and focuses on pins, answer “dolls” instead. Santería’s spirits are orishas, not lwa; Hoodoo has no priesthood at all.
trap.line: Real answer line: Voodoo [or Vodun; accept Haitian Vodou or Louisiana Voodoo]

topics.name: Yom Kippur
topics.kicker: Holiest day of the Jewish year · A 25-hour fast of repentance
topics.briefing: For about 25 hours, from sundown to nightfall the next day, many Jewish people go without food or water and spend hours in synagogue asking forgiveness for the past year’s wrongs. Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, is the holiest day of the Jewish year. It opens with the solemn Kol Nidre chant and ends with one long blast of a ram’s horn, the shofar.

sample.note: 13 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (3 Middle School/Easy High School + 10 Regular High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: Dodgers pitcher Sandy Koufax chose not to pitch the first game of the 1965 World Series because it fell on this holiday. On the day before this holiday, some people perform kapparot [“kah-pah-ROHT”] by swinging a chicken or a bag of coins over their heads, then giving it to the poor.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this holiest day of the Jewish year, a day of fasting and prayer that ends the High Holy Days.

tossups.p: In the 1927 film _The Jazz Singer_, often called the first “talkie,” Al Jolson’s character sings this holiday’s opening prayer at his synagogue in place of his father, a cantor who is too sick to sing. That prayer, Kol Nidre [“kohl NEE-dray”], means “All Vows” and is chanted mostly in Aramaic.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Jewish holy day that comes about ten days after Rosh Hashanah and includes a 25-hour fast.

tossups.p: Some men wear a white robe called a kittel [“KIT-ul”] on this holiday, and many other worshippers dress in white as a sign of purity. As this holiday begins, Torah scrolls are taken out of the ark and held while the cantor chants Kol Nidre [“kohl NEE-dray”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Jewish day of fasting and repentance, the last of the High Holy Days.

tossups.p: On this day only, the High Priest entered the Holy of Holies, the innermost room of the Temple in Jerusalem. He also spoke God’s four-letter name aloud, and the people who heard it bowed to the ground.
tossups.r: Today this holiday ends with the Ne’ila [“neh-ee-LAH”] service. For 10 points, name this Jewish holy day that falls on the tenth of Tishrei [“TISH-ray”].

tossups.p: Worshippers gently tap their chests while reciting the Ashamnu [“ah-SHAHM-noo”] and the Al Chet [“ahl KHET”], confession prayers that list sins in alphabetical order and say “we” instead of “I.” Those confessions are repeated throughout this holiday’s services.
tossups.r: Its final Ne’ila [“neh-ee-LAH”] service ends with a long blast of the shofar. For 10 points, name this holiest day of the Jewish year.

tossups.p: In the kapparot [“kah-pah-ROHT”] custom on the day before this holiday, some people swing a chicken or a bag of coins over their heads and then donate it to the poor. This holiday begins at sundown with the Kol Nidre [“kohl NEE-dray”] declaration.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Jewish holy day of fasting and prayer that ends the High Holy Days.

tossups.p: William Tyndale coined the English word “scapegoat” while translating a passage of Leviticus about this holiday, when lots were drawn over two goats. One goat was offered as a sacrifice, and the other was sent into the wilderness for Azazel [“uh-ZAY-zul”], symbolically carrying away the people’s sins.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this holiest day of the Jewish year, when the Book of Jonah is read.

tossups.p: Leviticus calls this holiday a “Sabbath of Sabbaths,” and it is the only Jewish fast day that is kept even when it falls on the Sabbath. Its services end with Ne’ila [“neh-ee-LAH”], a closing prayer said as the gates of heaven are imagined closing.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Jewish holiday of fasting, prayer, and atonement that follows Rosh Hashanah.

tossups.p: Jewish tradition says that on this date, Moses came down from Mount Sinai with the second set of tablets, a sign that the people had been forgiven for worshipping the golden calf. Tradition also says the Book of Life is sealed on this day.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Jewish holy day that ends the Ten Days of Repentance, which begin on Rosh Hashanah.

tossups.p: The words “Next year in Jerusalem,” which also end the Passover seder, are often said at the end of this holiday, along with a long blast of the shofar [“SHOH-far”]. They close its final service, Ne’ila [“neh-ee-LAH”], whose name means “locking,” as in the locking of heaven’s gates.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Jewish fast day that comes about ten days after Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish New Year.

tossups.p: This holiday has five prayer services, more than any other day of the Jewish year, from an evening service that opens with Kol Nidre [“kohl NEE-dray”] to Ne’ila [“neh-ee-LAH”] at sunset the next day. In its afternoon service, worshippers read the entire Book of Jonah.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Jewish day of fasting and repentance, which falls in September or October.

tossups.p: Golda Meir [“may-EER”] was Israel’s prime minister when Egypt and Syria launched a surprise attack on this holiday in October 1973, starting a war named for it. A goat ritual on this holiday, described in Leviticus, gave English the word “scapegoat.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this holiest day of the Jewish year, which ends the High Holy Days.

tossups.p: People greet each other on this holiday with a wish for “a good final sealing,” because tradition says each person’s fate for the coming year is written in the Book of Life at the new year and sealed on this day.
tossups.r: It ends the Ten Days of Repentance, or Days of Awe. For 10 points, name this Jewish fast day that falls on the tenth of Tishrei [“TISH-ray”].

tossups.p: On the afternoon of this holiday, worshippers read an entire biblical book about a prophet who is swallowed by a great fish after trying to run away from God’s command. That prophet finally warns the city of Nineveh, whose people repent and are spared.
tossups.r: That book is Jonah. For 10 points, name this Jewish fast day that begins with the Kol Nidre [“kohl NEE-dray”] prayer.

tossups.p: Many worshippers wear canvas sneakers on this holiday, because wearing leather shoes is one of five things that tradition forbids on this day. The other restrictions include eating and drinking, bathing, and putting on lotion or perfume.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this holiest day of the Jewish year, which ends the Ten Days of Repentance with a 25-hour fast.

trap.title: Which High Holy Day?
trap.body: Rosh Hashanah and this holiday are the two High Holy Days, and they share clues: the shofar, the Book of Life, the month of Tishrei, and the Days of Awe that link them. Tradition says your fate is written on Rosh Hashanah and sealed on Yom Kippur, so buzzing early on a Book of Life or shofar clue is risky. One Regular High School result also asks for the 1973 Yom Kippur War, a different answer line.
trap.fix: Rosh Hashanah is the New Year: apples and honey, tashlich, and many shofar blasts. Yom Kippur comes about ten days later: the 25-hour fast, Kol Nidre, Ne’ila, the Book of Jonah, kapparot, and the scapegoat. If the question asks for a war, the answer is the Yom Kippur War, not the holiday.
trap.line: Real answer line: Yom Kippur (accept Day of Atonement before it is read)

tossups.r: For 10 points, name this spring Jewish holiday that celebrates the Exodus, when Moses led the Israelites out of slavery in Egypt.

tossups.p: Since 1932, the Maxwell House coffee company has given away millions of copies of a guidebook for this holiday’s meal. That guidebook, the Haggadah [“huh-GAH-duh”], has a name meaning “telling,” and it includes the song “Dayenu” [“dye-AY-noo”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Jewish holiday when families hold a seder, eat matzah, and remember the Exodus from Egypt.

tossups.p: Near the end of this holiday’s ritual meal, people sing “Echad Mi Yodea” [“eh-KHAHD mee YOH-day-ah”] (“Who Knows One?”) and “Chad Gadya” [“KHAHD GAHD-yah”], an Aramaic song about one little goat that a father bought for two coins.
tossups.r: Earlier, people eat bitter herbs called maror [“mah-ROR”]. For 10 points, name this Jewish holiday that remembers the Exodus from Egypt.

tossups.p: The Haggadah [“huh-GAH-duh”] read at this holiday’s meal describes four sons: one wise, one wicked, one simple, and one who does not know how to ask. At that meal, the youngest child asks the Four Questions, including why everyone eats bitter herbs.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Jewish holiday that celebrates the Israelites’ escape from slavery in Egypt.

tossups.p: Hillel’s sandwich, eaten at this holiday’s meal, places bitter herbs between pieces of matzah. Charoset [“khah-ROH-set”], a sweet mix of apples, nuts, and wine, stands for the mortar the Israelites used to make bricks in Egypt.
tossups.r: Those foods sit on a special plate at the seder. For 10 points, name this Jewish holiday that celebrates the Exodus.

tossups.p: On the night before this holiday, families search their homes by candlelight for chametz [“khah-METS”], or leavened food, and they burn whatever they find the next morning. Some families formally sell any leftover leavened food to a non-Jew until the holiday ends.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Jewish holiday when matzah is eaten in place of bread and the Exodus is retold.

tossups.p: To make sure the dough never has time to rise, the flat bread for this holiday must be mixed and baked within 18 minutes. That bread recalls how the Israelites left in such a hurry that their dough could not rise.
tossups.r: That bread is matzah. For 10 points, name this Jewish holiday whose name comes from God “passing over” the Israelites’ homes.

tossups.p: Many Jews read the Song of Songs, a biblical poem full of springtime imagery, during this holiday, which begins on the 15th of Nisan [“nee-SAHN”]. The ritual meal on this holiday ends with the words “Next year in Jerusalem.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Jewish holiday that recalls Moses leading the Israelites out of Egypt.

tossups.p: In ancient times, this holiday was one of three pilgrimage festivals, along with Shavuot [“shah-voo-OHT”] and Sukkot [“soo-KOHT”], when people traveled to the Temple in Jerusalem. On this one, each household offered a lamb, which a roasted shank bone recalls today.
tossups.r: It sits on the seder plate with an egg and bitter herbs. For 10 points, name this Jewish holiday when matzah is eaten.

tossups.p: At this holiday’s meal, a special cup of wine is filled for the prophet Elijah, and the front door is opened to welcome him. Everyone drinks four cups of wine or grape juice during the meal.
tossups.r: Guests lean to one side as a sign of freedom. For 10 points, name this Jewish holiday that remembers the Exodus from Egypt.

tossups.p: The Gospels of Matthew, Mark, and Luke describe Jesus’s Last Supper as a meal for this holiday. In Greek and Latin, Easter is called “Pascha” [“PAHS-kah”], a word that comes from this holiday’s Hebrew name.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Jewish holiday when families eat matzah at a seder and retell the Exodus.

tossups.p: In the song “Dayenu” [“dye-AY-noo”], sung during this holiday’s meal, each verse names a gift from God and repeats that it “would have been enough.” That meal is called a seder, the Hebrew word for “order,” because it follows a set order of steps.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Jewish holiday when families eat matzah and retell how Moses led the Israelites out of Egypt.

tossups.p: During this holiday’s meal, people spill a drop of wine for each of the ten plagues, including blood, frogs, and locusts, to show that their joy is lessened by the Egyptians’ suffering. Those plagues struck Egypt after Pharaoh refused to let the Israelites go.
tossups.r: This holiday’s English name comes from the tenth plague, when God spared the Israelites’ homes. For 10 points, name this spring Jewish holiday celebrated with a seder.

tossups.p: Early in this holiday’s meal, people dip karpas [“KAR-pahs”], a green vegetable such as parsley, into salt water that stands for tears. Later, children hunt for the afikoman [“ah-fee-KOH-mahn”], a hidden piece of matzah that is the last food eaten that night.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Jewish holiday that recalls the Exodus from Egypt and lasts seven or eight days.

tossups.p: In the Book of Exodus, God tells the Israelites to eat the first meal of this holiday in a hurry, with their sandals on and walking staffs in hand, after marking their doorposts with a lamb’s blood. That meal came on the night of the tenth plague.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Jewish holiday when families hold a seder and eat matzah to remember the Exodus.

trap.title: The meal isn’t the holiday
trap.body: Almost every clue describes the seder, the ritual meal with the Haggadah, the Four Questions, and the afikoman, so it is tempting to buzz “seder.” But the seder is the meal held on the holiday’s first night (or first two nights), not the holiday itself, and real answer lines accept “Passover seder” but not “seder” alone. Clues about the Last Supper can also tempt you to say “Easter.”
trap.fix: Name the holiday: “Passover” or “Pesach.” Say “seder” only when the question asks for “this meal” or “this ritual dinner.” Shavuot comes seven weeks later (the giving of the Torah), and Sukkot is the fall harvest festival of huts.

media.note: Quick read: fasting, iftar, the Night of Power, and Eid al-Fitr

qb.tip: One of the eight results is a 2020 tossup whose answer was “fasting,” with this month used only as a clue, so read each answer line before you buzz.

sample.note: the 8 real QBReader tossups that came up for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked; 1 of them wanted “fasting”)

tossups.p: A verse in the Quran’s second surah, “The Cow,” says believers may eat and drink at night during this month until the white thread of dawn can be told apart from the black thread. The same surah calls this the month in which the Quran was sent down as guidance.
tossups.r: Each evening, families break the day’s fast with a meal called iftar. For 10 points, name this ninth month of the Islamic calendar, when Muslims fast from dawn to sunset.

tossups.p: During this month, many mosques hold extra night prayers called tarawih [“tah-rah-WEE”], and some recite one juz’ [“JOOZ”], or one-thirtieth of the Quran, each night so the whole book is finished by the month’s end. A meal called suhoor [“suh-HOOR”] is eaten before dawn on each day of this month.
tossups.r: It ends with the feast of Eid al-Fitr. For 10 points, name this Islamic holy month of daytime fasting.

tossups.p: On the 17th day of this month in the year 624, Muhammad’s outnumbered followers defeated an army from Mecca at the Battle of Badr [“BAH-der”]. Muslims believe the angel Gabriel first revealed the Quran to Muhammad during this month, on the Night of Power.
tossups.r: This month ends with the festival of Eid al-Fitr. For 10 points, name this ninth month of the Islamic year, when Muslims fast from dawn to sunset.

tossups.p: Egypt’s 1973 attack across the Suez Canal was code-named Operation Badr, and it began on the tenth day of this month, which that year fell on the Jewish holy day of Yom Kippur. That war is also named after this month, which includes the Night of Power.
tossups.r: Muslims eat a meal called iftar at sunset on each day of this month. For 10 points, name this Islamic holy month of fasting.

tossups.p: A short chapter of the Quran says that one night in this month is “better than a thousand months” and that angels come down on that night, which is peace until dawn. Many Muslims seek that night among the odd-numbered nights of this month’s last ten days, especially the 27th.
tossups.r: That night, Laylat al-Qadr [“LAY-lat al-KAH-der”], marks the first revelation of the Quran. For 10 points, name this Islamic month of fasting that ends with Eid al-Fitr.

tossups.p: Following Muhammad’s example, some Muslims spend the last ten days of this month in i’tikaf [“ih-tih-KAHF”], a retreat inside a mosque for prayer and reading the Quran. Those last ten nights are believed to include the Night of Power, when the Quran was first revealed.
tossups.r: Muslims eat suhoor before dawn and iftar after sunset during this month. For 10 points, name this ninth month of the Islamic calendar.

tossups.p: Before a special prayer at the end of this month, Muslims give a charity called zakat al-fitr [“zuh-KAHT al-FIT-er”] so that poor families can celebrate too. That celebration falls on the first day of Shawwal [“shah-WAHL”], the month that follows this one.
tossups.r: That festival, Eid al-Fitr, is the “Festival of Breaking the Fast.” For 10 points, name this Islamic holy month, when Muslims fast during daylight hours.

tossups.p: Muslims who miss days of this month’s main religious duty because of illness or travel must make them up later, and those who never can may instead give fidya [“FID-yah”] by feeding a needy person for each missed day. Young children and the elderly are excused from that duty.
tossups.r: That duty, the pillar of sawm, means fasting from dawn to sunset. For 10 points, name this ninth month of the Islamic calendar.

tossups.p: This month comes after Sha’ban [“shah-BAHN”] and before Shawwal [“shah-WAHL”]. Because it follows a lunar calendar, this month begins about 11 days earlier each year on the Gregorian calendar, so over about 33 years it passes through every season.
tossups.r: It ends with the feast of Eid al-Fitr. For 10 points, name this month in which Muslims fast from dawn to sunset.

tossups.p: Following a tradition that Muhammad broke his fast with dates and water, many Muslims begin their sunset meal during this month with a date. Before the first light of dawn, they eat another meal called suhoor [“suh-HOOR”].
tossups.r: That sunset meal is called iftar. For 10 points, name this ninth month of the Islamic calendar, whose fast is one of the Five Pillars of Islam.

tossups.p: In the year 630, Muhammad’s followers took control of Mecca with almost no fighting during this month. Six years earlier, also during this month, they had won the Battle of Badr [“BAH-der”]. Muslims believe the Quran was first revealed to Muhammad during this month.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Islamic holy month, which ends with the festival of Eid al-Fitr.

tossups.p: Muslims believe that during this month, while Muhammad was meditating in a cave on Mount Hira [“hih-RAH”], the angel Gabriel came to him and commanded him to “Read!” The Quran calls the night of that first revelation “better than a thousand months.”
tossups.r: Muslims mark this month by fasting from dawn to sunset. For 10 points, name this ninth month of the Islamic calendar.

tossups.p: The Quran tells believers that one practice “is prescribed to you as it was prescribed to those before you” and then names this month as the time for it. Travelers and the sick may skip that practice and make up the days later.
tossups.r: During this month, Muslims eat and drink nothing, not even water, from dawn until sunset. For 10 points, name this ninth month of the Islamic calendar.

tossups.p: A pillar of Islam whose Arabic name, sawm, means “to refrain” is mainly carried out during this month. Many Muslims also give extra charity during this month and try to read the entire Quran before it ends.
tossups.r: Each day of this month, Muslims eat suhoor before dawn and iftar after sunset. For 10 points, name this Islamic holy month of fasting.

tossups.p: In many countries, moon-sighting committees watch the western sky after sunset to spot the hilal [“hih-LAHL”], a thin crescent moon whose sighting begins and ends this month. As a result, this month lasts either 29 or 30 days, and its last ten nights include Laylat al-Qadr.
tossups.r: This month ends with the feast of Eid al-Fitr. For 10 points, name this ninth Islamic month, when Muslims fast from dawn to sunset.

clues.t: Ninth and holiest month of the Islamic calendar, which follows the moon
As an act of worship, Muslims fast from dawn to sunset each day: no food or drink, not even water
Ends with Eid al-Fitr, the “Festival of Breaking the Fast”
Each day’s fast is broken at sunset with a meal called iftar, often shared with family and friends
Its fast, called sawm (“to refrain”), is one of the Five Pillars of Islam, often listed fourth
Suhoor (or suhur) is the meal eaten before dawn, before the day’s fast begins
Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power, falls in its last ten nights; many observe it on the 27th
Muslims believe the angel Gabriel (Jibril) first revealed the Quran to Muhammad during this month
Children, the sick, travelers, the elderly, and pregnant or nursing mothers do not have to fast
Begins and ends with the sighting of a new crescent moon (hilal), so it lasts 29 or 30 days
The fast begins when a white thread can be told from a black thread at dawn, a rule from the surah “The Cow” (al-Baqarah)
The Quran says fasting “is prescribed to you as it was prescribed to those before you” (verse 2:183)
Tarawih: extra night prayers held in mosques during this month
Many mosques recite one juz’ (one-thirtieth of the Quran) each night, finishing the whole book by the month’s end
Comes after Sha’ban and before Shawwal, the month that begins with Eid al-Fitr
Many Muslims break each day’s fast by eating dates, following Muhammad’s example
Zakat al-Fitr: charity given before the Eid prayer so poor families can celebrate too
The Quran’s Surah al-Qadr says the Night of Power is “better than a thousand months”
I’tikaf: a retreat in a mosque for prayer during the last ten days, as Muhammad did
The Battle of Badr (624) and the conquest of Mecca (630) both took place during this month
Missed fast days are made up later; people who can never fast give fidya, feeding a needy person for each day
The 1973 war that began on Yom Kippur is also named for this month; Egypt called its attack Operation Badr

trap.title: Month, fast, or feast?
trap.body: The same clues (iftar, sawm, Eid al-Fitr) show up in tossups with different answers. One real 2020 tossup wanted “fasting,” the practice, and used this month only as a clue. Eid al-Fitr is the feast that ends the month, and real answer lines say do not accept Eid al-Adha, the Feast of the Sacrifice held during the Hajj season.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun. “This month” or “this period” means the month. “This action” or “this practice” means fasting (sawm). “This festival” or “this feast” means an Eid: breaking the fast and Shawwal point to Eid al-Fitr, while Abraham’s sacrifice and the Hajj point to Eid al-Adha.
trap.line: Real answer line: Ramadan [or Ramazan or Ramathan or Ramzan; prompt on Night of Power, Qadr Night, or Eid al-Fitr before they are read by asking “What longer period does that happen during?”; do NOT accept or prompt on “Eid al-Adha”]

sample.note: 13 real QBReader tossups (4 Middle School/Easy High School + 9 Regular High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: Bahá’u’lláh’s [“bah-HAH-oo-LAH”] _Kitáb-i-Aqdas_ [“kih-TAHB-ee AHK-dahs”] commands this practice, which Bahá’ís aged 15 to 70 observe from sunrise to sunset during ʻAláʼ [“ah-LAH”], the nineteen-day month just before their New Year, Naw-Rúz [“no-ROOZ”], in March.
tossups.r: Jews do it for about 25 hours on Yom Kippur. For 10 points, name this religious practice of going without food for a set time.

tossups.p: The 183rd verse of “The Cow,” the longest surah of the Qur’an, says that this practice was prescribed for believers as it was for those before them, so that they might gain taqwa [“TAHK-wah”], or God-consciousness.
tossups.r: Each day of it ends at sunset with a meal called iftar [“if-TAR”]. For 10 points, name this practice that Muslims observe during Ramadan.

tossups.p: On the first Sunday of most months, Latter-day Saints skip two meals and donate the money they save to help people in need. The Assyrian Church of the East does this for three days to remember how the people of Nineveh repented in the Book of Jonah.
tossups.r: Muslims do it every day of Ramadan. For 10 points, name this practice of going without food.

tossups.p: A stone statue from ancient Gandhara [“gun-DAR-uh”], now in the Lahore Museum, shows Siddhartha Gautama worn out by years of this practice. Siddhartha later gave up such harsh self-denial and chose the Middle Way.
tossups.r: Muslims do this from dawn to sunset during Ramadan. For 10 points, name this practice of going without food.

tossups.p: In January 1948, Mohandas Gandhi began this practice in Delhi and kept it up until community leaders promised to stop the fighting between Hindus and Muslims. Gandhi often used this action as a peaceful form of protest.
tossups.r: Muslims observe it during the daylight hours of Ramadan. For 10 points, name this practice of going without food.

tossups.p: Jews perform this practice on Tzom Gedaliah [“TSOHM ged-uh-LYE-uh”], the day after Rosh Hashanah, and on Ta’anit Esther [“tah-ah-NEET ESS-ter”], the day before Purim, which recalls Queen Esther asking her people to do this before she went to see the king.
tossups.r: On Tisha B’Av [“TISH-uh BAHV”], they do it while mourning the destroyed Temples in Jerusalem. For 10 points, name this practice also observed on Yom Kippur.

tossups.p: Jains call this practice upavasa [“oo-puh-VAH-suh”], and many perform it during Paryushana [“par-YOO-shuh-nuh”], a festival when they ask forgiveness from all living beings. During this practice, some Jains drink only boiled water.
tossups.r: Many Christians do this during Lent, the season before Easter. For 10 points, name this practice of giving up food for religious reasons.

tossups.p: On the holiday of Karva Chauth [“KUR-vuh CHOHT”], many married Hindu women perform this practice from sunrise until moonrise, praying for their husbands’ safety. Hindus also often do this on Ekadashi [“ay-KAH-duh-shee”], the eleventh day of each half of the lunar month, a day sacred to Vishnu.
tossups.r: Jews do it on Yom Kippur. For 10 points, name this religious practice of going without food.

tossups.p: Zoroastrians traditionally reject this practice, teaching that weakening the body makes a person less able to fight evil. The Guru Granth Sahib says that people who rely on this ritual are rewarded with “less than a shell.”
tossups.r: Many Christians perform it during Lent. For 10 points, name this practice that Muslims observe during the daylight hours of Ramadan.

tossups.p: An early Christian guidebook called the _Didache_ [“DID-uh-kay”] told believers to perform this practice on Wednesdays and Fridays, and John Wesley’s early Methodists kept that custom to remember the betrayal and death of Jesus.
tossups.r: Jesus himself did this for forty days in the wilderness. For 10 points, name this practice that many Christians observe during Lent.

tossups.p: A verse of the Qur’an says believers may eat and drink at night until the white thread of dawn can be told apart from the black thread, and then this practice begins. Travelers may skip this practice and make up the missed days later.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Pillar of Islam, which Muslims observe from dawn to sunset all through Ramadan.

tossups.p: Muslims are forbidden to do this on Eid al-Fitr [“EED al-FIT-ur”], the holiday that ends a month devoted to it. On each day of that month, believers eat a pre-dawn meal called suhoor [“suh-HOOR”] before starting this practice.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this practice, one of the Five Pillars of Islam, which lasts from dawn to sunset during Ramadan.

tossups.p: Jews perform this practice on Asara B’Tevet [“ah-SAH-rah buh-TAY-vet”], the tenth day of the month of Tevet, to remember when the Babylonians began their siege of Jerusalem. On the holiest day of the Jewish year, this practice lasts about 25 hours.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this practice that Jews observe on Yom Kippur and Muslims observe during Ramadan.

tossups.p: Moses performed this practice for forty days and forty nights on Mount Sinai while receiving the Ten Commandments. Many Muslims add six days of this practice in Shawwal [“shuh-WAHL”], the month after Ramadan.
tossups.r: Many Christians do it during Lent. For 10 points, name this practice of going without food for religious reasons.

tossups.p: Catholic rules for this practice allow one full meal plus two smaller meals that together do not equal a full one. Catholics aged 18 to 59 follow those rules on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday.
tossups.r: Many Christians do this during Lent, the 40 days before Easter. For 10 points, name this practice that Muslims observe during Ramadan, the ninth month of the Islamic calendar.

On Karva Chauth, many married Hindu women do it from sunrise to moonrise, praying for their husbands’ safety
Hindus often do it on Ekadashi, the 11th day of each half of the lunar month, a day sacred to Vishnu
Zoroastrians traditionally reject it, teaching that a weakened body is less able to fight evil
The Guru Granth Sahib says people who rely on this ritual are rewarded with “less than a shell”; Sikhism rejects it as a ritual
The Qur’an says each day of it begins when the white thread of dawn can be told apart from the black thread of night

trap.title: Practice or holy month?
trap.body: Fasting and Ramadan share almost every clue, but they are different answer lines. Real Ramadan tossups say “prompt on fasting or sawm” and then ask “What larger observance is that a part of?”, while fasting tossups use Ramadan, Yom Kippur, and Lent only as clues. One real tossup even wanted “eating” and said “do not accept or prompt on fasting.”
trap.fix: Listen to the noun. “This practice” or “this action” of going without food means fasting (or sawm). “This month” or “this observance,” with clues like the Night of Power or tarawih prayers, means Ramadan, and the holiday that ends it is Eid al-Fitr.
trap.line: Real answer lines: fasting [or sawm until it is read] and the month of Ramadan (prompt on “fasting” or “sawm” with “What larger observance is that a part of?”)

topics.name: Zen Buddhism
topics.kicker: Meditation school of Buddhism · Koans, zazen, and rock gardens
topics.briefing: Zen is a school of Buddhism built around sitting still and wrestling with riddles that have no easy answers. Legend says its founder, Bodhidharma, brought it from India to China and meditated facing a wall for nine years. In Japan, its monks practice zazen (seated meditation), puzzle over koans like the sound of one hand clapping, and rake gravel into rock gardens that look like rippling water.
topics.answerHtml: Zen Buddhism (accept Chan or Seon; prompt on Buddhism, Mahayana Buddhism, Rinzai, or Soto; do not accept other forms of Buddhism such as “Theravada” or “Tibetan Buddhism”)
