qb.tip: No Middle School or Easy High School tossups use this answer line, so the sample is 2 Regular High School ones; koans also lead off Buddhism and Mahayana tossups, so check whether the question wants this sect or the whole religion.

sample.note: 2 real QBReader tossups (0 Middle School/Easy High School + 2 Regular High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: When a teacher asked his students to write verses showing their understanding, an illiterate rice-pounder named Huineng [“hway-NUNG”] had a poem written on a wall saying there was nowhere for dust to land. Huineng became this school’s Sixth Patriarch, and his talks in the _Platform Sutra_ teach that enlightenment can come suddenly.
tossups.r: Its two main branches in Japan are Rinzai and Soto. For 10 points, name this meditation-centered school of Mahayana Buddhism.

tossups.p: After studying in China, the monk Dogen [“DOH-gen”] carried one branch of this school to Japan, founded the temple of Eiheiji [“ay-HAY-jee”], and wrote the _Shobogenzo_ [“shoh-boh-GEN-zoh”]. Dogen taught shikantaza [“shee-KAHN-tah-zah”], or “just sitting,” a kind of seated meditation that does not focus on a riddle or any other object.
tossups.r: Dogen’s branch is called Soto. For 10 points, name this school of Buddhism known for koans and zazen.

tossups.p: The monk Eisai [“AY-sye”] brought the Rinzai [“RIN-zye”] branch of this school from China to Japan and wrote a book praising the health benefits of drinking green tea. Later, the tea master Sen no Rikyu [“sen-noh-RIH-kyoo”], who trained in this school, shaped the simple, quiet style of the Japanese tea ceremony.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this school of Mahayana Buddhism famous for its koans and rock gardens.

tossups.p: The Japanese master Hakuin [“hah-koo-EEN”] revived the Rinzai [“RIN-zye”] branch of this school in the 1700s and created a famous riddle asking for the sound of one hand clapping. Riddles like that one, called koans [“KOH-ahnz”], are meant to jolt students out of ordinary logical thinking.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this school of Mahayana Buddhism whose followers practice seated meditation called zazen.

tossups.p: When a monk asked the master Zhaozhou [“JOW-joh”] whether a dog has Buddha-nature, Zhaozhou simply answered “Mu,” meaning “no” or “nothing.” That exchange opens _The Gateless Gate_, and the _Blue Cliff Record_ is another collection of such puzzling stories used by this school.
tossups.r: Those stories are called koans. For 10 points, name this school of Mahayana Buddhism that Bodhidharma brought to China.

tossups.p: At the Kyoto temple of Ryoan-ji [“ryoh-AHN-jee”], fifteen stones sit in a bed of raked white gravel, placed so that a visitor on the viewing porch can never see all fifteen at once. That dry landscape garden is the most famous of the rock gardens linked to this school.
tossups.r: Students of this school seek a sudden awakening called satori. For 10 points, name this school of Japanese Buddhism known for koans.

tossups.p: Masters of this school paint the ensō [“EN-soh”], a circle drawn in a single brushstroke, as a sign of enlightenment and of a mind set free. The monk Sesshu [“SESS-shoo”], one of Japan’s greatest ink painters, trained in this school.
tossups.r: Its students seek satori, or awakening. For 10 points, name this school of Buddhism famous in Japan for koans and rock gardens.

tossups.p: Round, red Daruma [“DAH-roo-mah”] dolls, whose blank eyes are filled in when someone sets and then reaches a goal, are modeled on this school’s founder. That founder is said to have meditated while facing a cave wall for nine years near the Shaolin [“shau-LIN”] Temple.
tossups.r: That founder, Bodhidharma, is said to have brought this school from India to China. For 10 points, name this meditation school of Mahayana Buddhism.

tossups.p: When Emperor Wu of Liang [“lee-AHNG”] asked how much merit he had earned by building temples and copying scriptures, this school’s founder is said to have told him he had earned none at all. That founder, called the “Blue-Eyed Barbarian” in some Chinese texts, is shown in art as a fierce, bearded monk.
tossups.r: Daruma dolls are modeled on that founder, Bodhidharma. For 10 points, name this school of Mahayana Buddhism that uses koans.

tossups.p: This school’s name comes, by way of Chinese, from the Sanskrit word dhyana [“DYAH-nuh”], meaning “meditation.” In one branch of this school, meditators sit facing a wall, and a teacher may tap a sleepy student’s shoulders with a flat wooden stick called a keisaku [“KAY-sah-koo”].
tossups.r: That seated meditation is called zazen. For 10 points, name this school of Buddhism popular in Japan.

tossups.p: Martin Luther King Jr. nominated the Vietnamese monk Thich Nhat Hanh [“tick-nyaht-HAHN”], a teacher in this tradition, for the Nobel Peace Prize in 1967. Thich Nhat Hanh later founded the Plum Village community in France and wrote popular books such as _The Miracle of Mindfulness_.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this meditation school of Mahayana Buddhism that Bodhidharma is said to have brought to China.

tossups.p: The poet Matsuo Basho [“BAH-shoh”], who wrote a famous haiku about a frog jumping into an old pond, studied meditation in this tradition. The German professor Eugen Herrigel [“HAIR-ih-gul”] wrote a well-known book about how learning Japanese archery taught him this school’s ideas.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this school of Buddhism popular in Japan, whose two main branches are Rinzai and Soto.

tossups.p: The Japanese scholar D. T. Suzuki’s English-language books made this school famous in the West, where it later fascinated writers of the Beat Generation. Jack Kerouac’s novel _The Dharma Bums_ features Japhy Ryder, a character based on the poet Gary Snyder, who went to Japan to study this school.
tossups.r: It began in China, where it absorbed ideas from Daoism. For 10 points, name this school of Buddhism that uses koans and seated meditation.

tossups.p: During Japan’s Kamakura [“kah-mah-KOO-rah”] period, this school won strong support from samurai warriors, who admired its discipline. Japan’s rulers later ranked its leading temples in a “Five Mountains” system, and Kyoto’s Golden Pavilion, or Kinkaku-ji [“KEEN-kah-koo-jee”], is a temple of this school.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this school of Buddhism whose major branches in Japan are Rinzai and Soto.

tossups.p: The Chinese master Linji [“lin-JEE”], whose name is pronounced Rinzai in Japanese, was famous for sudden shouts meant to startle students into awakening. Long before Linji, a monk named Huike [“hway-KUH”] became this school’s Second Patriarch as the successor of its founder.
tossups.r: That founder, Bodhidharma, is said to have brought this school to China. For 10 points, name this meditation school of Mahayana Buddhism known for koans.

clues.t: A school of Mahayana Buddhism that is especially popular in Japan
Students puzzle over koans, riddles meant to break ordinary logical thinking
Its name means “meditation”; its seated meditation is called zazen
Famous for dry rock gardens of stones and raked gravel
Its founder, Bodhidharma, is said to have brought it from India to China; his successor Huike was the Second Patriarch
Two main branches in Japan: Rinzai (uses koans) and Soto (“just sitting”)
Seeks satori, a sudden awakening; enlightenment can come all at once
Round, red Daruma dolls are modeled on Bodhidharma; you fill in one eye for a goal and the other when you reach it
Began in China, where it absorbed ideas from Daoism, then spread to Korea, Vietnam, and Japan
Shaped Japanese arts: haiku (Matsuo Basho), ink painting (Sesshu), calligraphy, archery, and the tea ceremony
Huineng, the illiterate Sixth Patriarch, won a verse contest; his _Platform Sutra_ teaches sudden enlightenment
Dogen brought the Soto branch to Japan, founded Eiheiji temple, wrote the _Shobogenzo_, and taught shikantaza (“just sitting”)
Eisai brought the Rinzai branch to Japan and praised green tea; tea master Sen no Rikyu trained in this school
Hakuin revived the Rinzai branch in the 1700s and invented the riddle about the sound of one hand clapping
Koan collections: _The Gateless Gate_ (opening with Zhaozhou’s answer “Mu”) and the _Blue Cliff Record_
Ryoan-ji in Kyoto: 15 stones in raked white gravel, placed so you can never see all 15 at once from the porch
The ensō: a circle painted in one brushstroke, a sign of enlightenment
Bodhidharma, the “Blue-Eyed Barbarian,” told Emperor Wu he had earned no merit and is said to have faced a wall for nine years near Shaolin
Its name comes from Sanskrit dhyana (“meditation”) by way of Chinese; a keisaku stick taps sleepy meditators
Vietnamese monk Thich Nhat Hanh, nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize by Martin Luther King Jr., founded Plum Village in France
D. T. Suzuki spread it in the West; Jack Kerouac’s _The Dharma Bums_ features Japhy Ryder, based on poet Gary Snyder
Popular with samurai in the Kamakura period; its temples include the “Five Mountains” and Kyoto’s Golden Pavilion (Kinkaku-ji)
Chinese master Linji (Rinzai in Japanese) used sudden shouts to startle students into awakening

trap.title: Koans don’t always mean Zen
trap.body: Koans are this school’s most famous clue, but they also open Buddhism tossups (“one sect of this religion uses koans”) and Mahayana tossups, where Zen is only one school inside a bigger branch. The middle school Buddhism answer lines accept only “Buddhism,” and a real Mahayana line just prompts on “Zen.” On Zen’s own tossups, saying “Buddhism” or “Mahayana Buddhism” only earns a prompt.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this sect” or “this school” plus Bodhidharma, Dogen, zazen, satori, or Japanese rock gardens means Zen. “This religion,” or a branch whose name means “Great Vehicle,” means Buddhism or Mahayana. If you get prompted after saying “Buddhism,” add “Zen.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Zen Buddhism [accept Chan Buddhism; prompt on “Buddhism” or “Mahayana Buddhism”; do NOT accept any other forms of Buddhism]

topics.name: Diwali
topics.kicker: Hindu festival of lights · Honors Lakshmi and Rama’s homecoming
topics.briefing: Every autumn, families across India and around the world light rows of little clay lamps called diyas, set off fireworks, share sweets, and draw colorful rangoli designs at their doors. Many Hindus remember how Prince Rama returned home to Ayodhya with Sita after defeating the demon king Ravana, and they welcome Lakshmi, the goddess of wealth. Sikhs and Jains mark their own holidays at the same time.
topics.answerHtml: Diwali (accept Deepavali, Divali, Dipavali, Deepawali, or the Nepali name Tihar; prompt on “Festival of Lights” or on single days like “Bhai Dooj”; do not accept “Holi,” “Hanukkah,” or “Navaratri”)

qb.tip: All 9 real tossups mention Lakshmi and end with the “festival of lights” nickname, and most also use diyas, rangoli, and Rama’s return, so those are must-know clues.

sample.note: 9 real QBReader tossups (3 Middle School/Easy High School + 6 Regular High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: Jains celebrate this holiday as the anniversary of the nirvana of Mahavira [“muh-HAH-vee-ruh”], the last tirthankara [“teer-TUN-kuh-ruh”], who reached liberation at Pawapuri [“PAH-vah-poo-ree”]. Like the Hindu version of this holiday, the Jain one falls on the new moon night of the month of Kartika [“KAR-tee-kuh”].
tossups.r: Hindus light clay lamps called diyas on this holiday. For 10 points, name this autumn festival of lights.

tossups.p: Sikhs celebrate Bandi Chhor Divas [“BUN-dee CHOR dee-VAHS”] at the same time as this holiday, remembering how Guru Hargobind [“HAR-goh-bind”] was freed from Gwalior [“GWAH-lee-or”] Fort along with 52 imprisoned princes. On that day, Sikhs light up the Golden Temple in Amritsar.
tossups.r: Hindus honor the goddess Lakshmi during this holiday. For 10 points, name this Hindu festival of lights.

tossups.p: The second day of this holiday, Naraka Chaturdashi [“NUH-ruh-kuh chuh-toor-DUSH-ee”], celebrates the god Krishna’s defeat of the demon Narakasura [“nuh-ruh-KAH-soo-ruh”]. In South India, many families begin that day with an oil bath before sunrise, followed by new clothes and sweets.
tossups.r: Families draw rangoli designs at their doors during this festival. For 10 points, name this five-day Hindu festival of lights.

tossups.p: On Dhanteras [“dun-TAIR-us”], the first day of this holiday, many families buy new pots, utensils, or gold, and some honor Dhanvantari [“dun-VUN-tuh-ree”], the god of medicine. This holiday’s main night falls on the new moon of the month of Kartika [“KAR-tee-kuh”].
tossups.r: That night honors Lakshmi, the goddess of wealth. For 10 points, name this Hindu festival of lights, usually held in October or November.

tossups.p: In Nepal, one day of this five-day festival honors crows, another honors dogs with flower garlands and treats, and another honors cows. On the festival’s last day there, sisters place colorful tika [“TEE-kuh”] marks on their brothers’ foreheads and pray for their long lives.
tossups.r: In India, this holiday recalls Rama’s return to Ayodhya. For 10 points, name this Hindu festival of lights.

tossups.p: On Bhai Dooj [“BYE DOOJ”], the last day of this holiday, sisters pray for their brothers’ long lives, and brothers often visit their sisters’ homes for a meal. The day before, many Hindus perform Govardhan Puja, remembering how Krishna lifted a hill to shelter villagers from a storm.
tossups.r: This holiday’s main night honors Lakshmi. For 10 points, name this festival of lights celebrated with diyas and rangoli.

tossups.p: Many temples prepare Annakut [“UN-uh-koot”], a “mountain of food” offered to Krishna, during this holiday. In Gujarat [“goo-juh-RAHT”], the new year begins right after this holiday’s main night, and many merchants worship fresh account books for the coming business year.
tossups.r: Families light lamps to welcome Lakshmi, goddess of wealth. For 10 points, name this Hindu festival of lights.

tossups.p: In West Bengal, many Hindus worship the fierce goddess Kali [“KAH-lee”] on this holiday’s new moon night, while most other regions worship Lakshmi. Bengali families often buy and share sweets such as sandesh [“SHUN-desh”] for the celebration.
tossups.r: Homes glow with rows of clay lamps called diyas. For 10 points, name this Hindu festival of lights.

tossups.p: For this holiday, families draw rangoli [“run-GOH-lee”], colorful floor designs made from powders, rice, or flower petals, at their doorways to welcome guests. In Tamil Nadu, similar designs called kolam [“KOH-lum”] are drawn with rice flour.
tossups.r: This holiday honors Lakshmi and celebrates Rama’s homecoming. For 10 points, name this Hindu festival of lights held in October or November.

tossups.p: On this holiday’s main night, many families leave doors and windows open and light lamps so that a goddess who sits on a lotus and rides an owl will visit their homes. That goddess is often worshiped alongside Ganesha [“guh-NAY-shuh”], the elephant-headed remover of obstacles.
tossups.r: That goddess is Lakshmi, and families draw rangoli at their doors to welcome her. For 10 points, name this Hindu festival of lights.

tossups.p: Many Hindus say this holiday recalls how the people of Ayodhya [“uh-YOHD-hyuh”] lit rows of lamps to welcome their prince home after fourteen years of exile and his victory over the demon king Ravana [“RAH-vuh-nuh”]. That prince returned with his wife, Sita, his brother Lakshmana [“LUK-shmuh-nuh”], and the monkey hero Hanuman.
tossups.r: That prince was Rama, and today families still light clay lamps called diyas. For 10 points, name this Hindu festival of lights.

tossups.p: In Maharashtra [“mah-huh-RAHSH-truh”], families hang star-shaped paper lanterns called kandils [“kun-DEELZ”] outside their homes for this holiday and make snacks and sweets such as chakli [“CHUCK-lee”] and karanji [“kuh-RUN-jee”]. Many people also wear new clothes and set off fireworks.
tossups.r: The holiday’s main day honors the goddess Lakshmi. For 10 points, name this Hindu festival of lights.

tossups.p: This holiday’s name comes from Sanskrit words meaning “row of lamps.” Families line their windows, doorsteps, and rooftops with those lamps, which stand for the victory of light over darkness and of good over evil.
tossups.r: The small clay oil lamps are called diyas. For 10 points, name this Hindu festival of lights, which honors Lakshmi.

tossups.p: This festival’s main night falls on amavasya [“uh-MAH-vus-yuh”], the darkest, moonless night of the Hindu month of Kartika [“KAR-tee-kuh”], about three weeks after the festival of Dussehra [“duh-SAIR-uh”]. Its date changes from year to year because Hindu months follow the moon.
tossups.r: Families light diyas and draw rangoli. For 10 points, name this five-day Hindu festival of lights in October or November.

tossups.p: This holiday is a national public holiday in Trinidad and Tobago, Guyana, Fiji, and Mauritius, and the English city of Leicester [“LESS-ter”] hosts one of the largest celebrations of it outside India. Singapore’s Little India neighborhood is decorated with bright lights for it each year.
tossups.r: It honors Lakshmi and celebrates Rama’s return to Ayodhya. For 10 points, name this Hindu festival of lights.

clues.t: Nicknamed the “festival of lights”; one of the biggest Hindu holidays
Honors Lakshmi, the goddess of wealth and good fortune
Families light diyas, small clay oil lamps, in rows
Celebrated in autumn, usually in October or November
Recalls Rama’s return to Ayodhya with Sita after 14 years of exile and his defeat of Ravana
Families draw rangoli, colorful floor designs of powder, rice, or petals (called kolam in Tamil Nadu)
Lasts five days; the third and main day is Lakshmi Puja
People share sweets (mithai), wear new clothes, and set off fireworks
Lakshmi, who sits on a lotus and rides an owl, is worshiped with Ganesha; doors are left open for her
Main night: amavasya, the new moon of the month of Kartika
Second day, Naraka Chaturdashi: Krishna’s defeat of the demon Narakasura; South Indians take a pre-dawn oil bath
Last day, Bhai Dooj: sisters pray for their brothers, who visit them for a meal
Begins a new business year: merchants worship new account books, and Gujarat’s new year starts the next day
Jains mark Mahavira’s nirvana at Pawapuri on the same night
Sikhs celebrate Bandi Chhor Divas: Guru Hargobind was freed from Gwalior Fort with 52 princes
First day, Dhanteras: people buy pots, utensils, or gold and honor Dhanvantari, god of medicine
In Nepal, its days honor crows, dogs, and cows, and sisters put tika marks on their brothers’ foreheads
Fourth day: Govardhan Puja and Annakut (“mountain of food”), remembering Krishna lifting a hill; also called Padwa
In West Bengal, the fierce goddess Kali is worshiped on its new moon night
In Maharashtra, families hang star-shaped kandil lanterns and make snacks like chakli
Its name comes from Sanskrit for “row of lamps”; the lamps stand for light beating darkness and good beating evil
Comes about three weeks after Dussehra, the festival of Rama’s victory over Ravana
A public holiday in Trinidad and Tobago, Guyana, Fiji, and Mauritius; Leicester, England, holds a huge celebration

trap.title: Which festival of lights?
trap.body: Hanukkah, the Jewish holiday, is also called the Festival of Lights, so real Diwali answer lines only prompt on “festival of lights” until the nickname is read. Diwali also gets mixed up with other Hindu festivals: Holi is the spring festival of colors, while Navaratri and Dussehra come a few weeks before Diwali. Sikhs celebrate Bandi Chhor Divas on the same day, but that is its own answer.
trap.fix: Hanukkah clues: a menorah, eight nights, the Maccabees, and dreidels. Diwali clues: diyas, rangoli, Lakshmi, Rama’s return to Ayodhya, and the month of Kartika. If you are prompted after saying “festival of lights,” name the holiday: Diwali.
trap.line: Real answer line: Diwali (accept Divali; accept Deepavali; prompt on “Festival of Lights” before it is read)

Over several days they walk seven times around the Kaaba, pray on the plain of Arafat, and throw pebbles at pillars that stand for the devil. sample.note: 8 real QBReader tossups (4 Middle School/Easy High School + 4 Regular High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: Participants in this event repeatedly chant the Talbiyah [“tal-BEE-yah”], a prayer that begins “Here I am, O God, here I am.” Before starting, men put on two plain white cloths to enter a holy state called ihram [“ih-RAHM”], in which hunting and wearing perfume are forbidden.
tossups.r: Pilgrims later walk seven times around the Kaaba. For 10 points, name this annual Islamic pilgrimage to Mecca.

tossups.p: Travelers to this event must enter a state of purity called ihram [“ih-RAHM”] before crossing boundary points called miqat [“mee-KAHT”]. In that state, they may not cut their hair, argue, or hunt, and men wear two seamless white garments so that rich and poor look the same.
tossups.r: Participants walk seven times between the hills of Safa and Marwah. For 10 points, name this pilgrimage to Mecca, the fifth pillar of Islam.

tossups.p: In 1324, Mansa Musa of Mali set out on this journey with a huge caravan and gave away so much gold in Cairo that the metal’s value there fell for years. During this journey, participants throw pebbles at three pillars in the Stoning of the Devil.
tossups.r: Pilgrims also circle the Kaaba seven times. For 10 points, name this pilgrimage to Mecca, one of the Five Pillars of Islam.

tossups.p: After making this journey in 1964, Malcolm X wrote that he had seen people of every color worshipping together as equals, and he took a new Muslim name. Participants in this journey drink water from the Zamzam [“ZAHM-zahm”] well.
tossups.r: They also walk around the Kaaba in the Masjid al-Haram [“MAS-jid al-hah-RAHM”]. For 10 points, name this annual pilgrimage to Mecca.

tossups.p: In 1325, a 21-year-old Ibn Battuta left Tangier to make this journey, beginning nearly 30 years of travel that he later described in his _Rihla_. Many people on this journey camp in a huge tent city at Mina.
tossups.r: Its rites include the Stoning of the Devil and circling the Kaaba. For 10 points, name this Islamic pilgrimage to Mecca.

tossups.p: Participants in this event spend a night under the open sky at Muzdalifah [“mooz-DAH-lih-fah”], where many gather the pebbles they will later throw at three pillars that stand for the devil. That stoning ritual takes place at the Jamarat [“jah-mah-RAHT”] Bridge.
tossups.r: Every Muslim who is able must make this journey at least once. For 10 points, name this pilgrimage to Mecca.

tossups.p: On the most important day of this event, participants stand in prayer from noon to sunset on a plain near the Mount of Mercy, where Muhammad gave his Farewell Sermon in 632. That day, the Day of Arafat, falls on the ninth of Dhu al-Hijjah [“DOO al-HIJ-ah”].
tossups.r: The next day begins the festival of Eid al-Adha. For 10 points, name this pilgrimage to Mecca, the fifth pillar of Islam.

tossups.p: During this event, participants try to kiss or touch the Black Stone, which is set into one corner of a shrine, or simply point toward it as they pass in huge crowds. They circle that shrine seven times in a counterclockwise ritual called tawaf [“tah-WAHF”].
tossups.r: That shrine is the Kaaba. For 10 points, name this pilgrimage to Mecca that Muslims who are able must make once in their lives.

tossups.p: Near the end of this event, men shave their heads in a rite called halq [“HALK”] or trim their hair in a rite called taqsir [“tahk-SEER”], which lets them leave the holy state of ihram. Before that, they throw pebbles at a pillar in the valley of Mina.
tossups.r: Participants also drink from the Zamzam well. For 10 points, name this Islamic pilgrimage to Mecca, held every year.

tossups.p: A shorter version of this ritual, called the Umrah [“OOM-rah”], can be performed at any time of year, but this ritual itself takes place only on set days each year. Both rituals include walking seven times between the hills of Safa and Marwah.
tossups.r: This ritual also includes the Stoning of the Devil. For 10 points, name this annual pilgrimage to Mecca, one of the Five Pillars of Islam.

tossups.p: In a rite of this event called sa’i [“SAH-ee”], participants walk seven times between the hills of Safa [“SAH-fah”] and Marwah [“MAR-wah”], remembering Hagar’s desperate search for water for her baby son, Ishmael. Muslims believe that search ended when the Zamzam well appeared.
tossups.r: Participants in this event also circle the Kaaba. For 10 points, name this pilgrimage to Mecca, the fifth pillar of Islam.

tossups.p: In the days after Eid al-Adha begins, people taking part in this event throw seven pebbles at each of three pillars at the Jamarat [“jah-mah-RAHT”] Bridge in Mina, recalling how Muslims believe Abraham drove Satan away. Many of them stay in a giant tent city nearby.
tossups.r: That ritual is the Stoning of the Devil. For 10 points, name this annual pilgrimage to Mecca.

tossups.p: Muslims believe that Abraham and his son Ishmael built the shrine at the center of this event as a house for worshipping one God. Muhammad performed this event only once, in 632, a few months before his death.
tossups.r: Participants wear simple white clothing called ihram and circle the Kaaba. For 10 points, name this pilgrimage to Mecca, the fifth pillar of Islam.

tossups.p: Muslims believe that a well called Zamzam [“ZAHM-zahm”] miraculously appeared in the desert to save Hagar and her baby Ishmael, and participants in this event drink its water and often carry some home. This event’s rites include walking between Safa and Marwah to remember Hagar’s search.
tossups.r: Participants also circle the Kaaba seven times inside the Great Mosque. For 10 points, name this annual pilgrimage to Mecca.

tossups.p: A black cloth embroidered with gold, called the kiswah [“KISS-wah”], covers the cube-shaped shrine at the center of this event and is replaced every year. That shrine sits in the courtyard of the Masjid al-Haram [“MAS-jid al-hah-RAHM”], the Great Mosque.
tossups.r: Eid al-Adha is celebrated during this event, whose participants circle the Kaaba seven times. For 10 points, name this pilgrimage to Mecca, one of the Five Pillars of Islam.

trap.title: Hajj, Umrah, or Pillars?
trap.body: The Umrah is a shorter “lesser pilgrimage” to Mecca that can happen at any time of year, and it shares rites like ihram, tawaf, and sa’i. Real answer lines disagree on it: two accept “Umrah” only before it is mentioned, and one says do not accept or prompt on it. Two real SCOP tossups about ihram and circling the Kaaba actually wanted the Five Pillars of Islam, and their answer line asks a player who says “hajj” to be less specific.
trap.fix: Say “Hajj,” not “Umrah”: a clue like “a shorter version of this” or “at any time of year” describes the Umrah, so the answer is the Hajj itself. If the question asks for a “set” of principles and names sawm or salat, say Five Pillars. Don’t confuse the Hajj with the Hijra, Muhammad’s move to Medina in 622.
trap.line: Real answer line: Hajj (prompt on pilgrimage, do not accept or prompt on “Umrah”)

topics.briefing: In the Bible’s story, baby Moses floated in a basket on the Nile until an Egyptian princess pulled him out of the water. In the Book of Exodus, he grows up to confront Pharaoh, leads the Israelites out of slavery through the parted Red Sea, and carries the Ten Commandments down from Mount Sinai. Jews, Christians, and Muslims all honor him as a great prophet; in Arabic his name is Musa.

sample.note: the 7 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: When the Israelites found only bitter water at Marah [“MAR-uh”], this man threw a piece of wood into it, and the water turned sweet. At Rephidim [“REF-ih-dim”], he struck a rock with his staff so that water poured out for his thirsty followers.
tossups.r: While he was away on a mountain, his brother Aaron made a golden calf. For 10 points, name this prophet who led the Israelites out of Egypt.

tossups.p: Statues of Rachel and Leah stand on either side of Michelangelo’s marble sculpture of this man on the tomb of Pope Julius II in Rome. That seated statue has two small horns, because an old Latin translation of the Bible said this man’s face was “horned” instead of “shining.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this biblical figure who carried two tablets with the Ten Commandments down from Mount Sinai.

tossups.p: When poisonous snakes bit the Israelites in the wilderness, this man set a bronze serpent on a pole, and anyone who looked at it was healed. His father-in-law, Jethro, visited his camp and advised him to appoint judges to help settle the people’s disputes.
tossups.r: His wife, Zipporah, was Jethro’s daughter. For 10 points, name this leader whose people crossed the Red Sea on dry land.

tossups.p: In the Quran’s chapter called “The Cave,” this prophet travels with a wise servant of God, whom tradition names Khidr [“KID-er”], who warns him that he will not have the patience to follow him. The Quran names this prophet more often than any other person.
tossups.r: In the Bible, he receives the Ten Commandments on Mount Sinai. For 10 points, name this prophet who led the Israelites out of Egypt.

tossups.p: After speaking with God, this man’s face shone so brightly that he covered it with a veil when he talked to the people. Earlier, during his forty days on a mountain, his brother made an idol for the impatient people waiting below.
tossups.r: When he saw the people dancing around that golden calf, he smashed the stone tablets. For 10 points, name this prophet who received the Ten Commandments on Mount Sinai.

tossups.p: After shepherds drove seven sisters away from a well in Midian [“MID-ee-un”], this man helped them water their flock, and he later married one of them, Zipporah. He had fled to Midian after killing an Egyptian whom he saw beating a Hebrew slave.
tossups.r: Years later, God spoke to him from a burning bush. For 10 points, name this prophet who returned to Egypt to free the Israelites.

tossups.p: When this man asked what name he should use for God, he was told, “I am who I am.” This man protested that he was “slow of speech,” so God chose his older brother to speak for him.
tossups.r: That brother was Aaron, and the conversation took place at a burning bush. For 10 points, name this prophet whom God sent to tell Pharaoh, “Let my people go.”

tossups.p: The Bible explains this man’s name with the words “I drew him out of the water.” His mother, Jochebed [“JOCK-uh-bed”], hid him in a basket coated with tar among the reeds, and his sister watched over him from a distance. In the Quran, Pharaoh’s wife asks to keep the baby.
tossups.r: In the Bible, Pharaoh’s daughter found the basket while bathing in the Nile. For 10 points, name this baby who grew up to lead the Exodus.

tossups.p: God told this man to speak to a rock to bring out water, but he struck it twice with his staff instead, so God said he would not lead the people into their new land. Later, from Mount Nebo [“NEE-boh”], he saw that Promised Land before dying at age 120.
tossups.r: His assistant Joshua then led the Israelites into Canaan. For 10 points, name this prophet of the Exodus.

tossups.p: Pharaoh’s magicians copied some wonders that this man and his brother performed, such as turning a staff into a snake, but they could not copy the plague of gnats. Plagues of hail, locusts, and darkness followed whenever Pharaoh refused this man’s demand.
tossups.r: The Jewish holiday of Passover remembers the escape from Egypt that he led. For 10 points, name this prophet who told Pharaoh, “Let my people go.”

tossups.p: A pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night guided this man’s people out of Egypt. After his people reached safety on the far shore, his sister Miriam picked up a tambourine and led the women in a song of victory.
tossups.r: Pharaoh’s chariots had been swept away by the returning waters. For 10 points, name this leader who parted the Red Sea.

tossups.p: Every morning except on the Sabbath, this leader’s followers gathered a flaky food called manna, which they ate for forty years in the wilderness. Twelve spies he sent into Canaan returned with a giant cluster of grapes.
tossups.r: Only Joshua and Caleb urged the people to enter that land. For 10 points, name this man who received the Ten Commandments on Mount Sinai.

tossups.p: In the Gospels, this man and Elijah appear beside Jesus on a mountain during the Transfiguration. The Gospel of John says that the law was given through this man, but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.
tossups.r: Jews traditionally credit him with writing the Torah. For 10 points, name this prophet who received the Ten Commandments on Mount Sinai.

tossups.p: During a battle against the Amalekites [“AM-uh-leck-ites”] at Rephidim, the Israelites were winning only while this man held his hands up, so Aaron and Hur held up his tired arms until sunset. Joshua led the fighting in that battle.
tossups.r: Before that, ten plagues had struck Egypt when Pharaoh refused to free the Israelites. For 10 points, name this prophet who parted the Red Sea.

tossups.p: Charlton Heston played this man in a 1956 Cecil B. DeMille epic, and Val Kilmer voiced him in the 1998 animated film _The Prince of Egypt_. Rembrandt painted this man raising two stone tablets high above his head.
tossups.r: In the Book of Exodus, he leads the Israelites out of slavery. For 10 points, name this prophet who parted the Red Sea.

trap.title: Moses or his brother?
trap.body: Many Moses clues are about his family, and early buzzers grab the wrong name. Aaron, his older brother, spoke for him before Pharaoh and made the golden calf; Miriam, his sister, led the song after the Red Sea crossing. If you hear “this man’s brother made a golden calf,” the answer is Moses, not Aaron. Joshua (who led the people into Canaan) and Elijah (who also met God on Mount Horeb) are traps too.
trap.fix: Listen for “this man’s brother” or “this man’s sister.” Smashing the tablets is Moses; making the calf is Aaron; the walls of Jericho are Joshua. In questions about Islam he is called Musa, which is accepted.
